conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted for nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been feeling sick for about two days. Started after I ate a grapefruit. I’ve been nauseous and throwing up, but no belly pain. Just feel bloated and tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever, cough, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or chest issues. I did feel a bit off a week ago, but that passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll run some tests. Your vitals are stable, and your exam looks good—no tenderness in the belly. We’ll start IV fluids since you haven’t been keeping much down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been on G-tube feeds for years because of swallowing issues. Should I stop those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold the G-tube feeds for now and give you fluids through the IV. We’ll check your labs and see how you do with small sips later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work shows your kidney function is a bit worse—creatinine is 2.1, up from your baseline of 1.5 or 1.6. This is likely from not drinking enough due to vomiting. The IV fluids should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know my kidneys were involved. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s what we call pre-renal—meaning it’s due to low volume, not kidney damage. As you rehydrate, it should improve. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about the nausea? I’ve been on Bactrim for a UTI—could that be causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. Bactrim can cause stomach upset. But we’re also checking for infection. Your urine test showed blood and signs of infection, so we’re treating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I finished the Bactrim course already. Do I need more antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re waiting on the urine culture. If it confirms infection, you may need another course. We’ll decide once we get the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray shows mildly distended bowel loops, but no blockage. It’s nonspecific—could be from the nausea or reduced movement from being unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blockage is good. Can I try eating something small?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try clear liquids. Start with water or broth. If you keep that down, we’ll advance slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—no vomiting since this morning. Your repeat labs show your kidney function is already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go back on my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted your mycophenolate, prednisone, and pain meds. We’re avoiding Zofran for nausea because of your long QT, but Ativan is helping and is safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, my heart condition. I’ve had torsades before. So no Zofran—got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood cultures came back clean. No bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture grew Proteus mirabilis, which matches your earlier UTIs. It’s sensitive to Bactrim, which you’ve tolerated before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I need more antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll send you home with a 7-day course of Bactrim. Even though you finished one recently, this ensures the infection clears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave a small dose of IV ceftriaxone earlier, but you developed itching in your hands. We gave Benadryl, and it’s improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my hands got really itchy. Is that an allergy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You’re already allergic to penicillins and ciprofloxacin, so we’ll note ceftriaxone as a possible allergy. We’ll avoid it in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve had reactions before. What about the rash on my neck?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s faint and improving. Could be related to the ceftriaxone or just a mild skin reaction. Keep an eye on it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look much better. Creatinine is down to 1.6—back to your baseline. You’ve kept down food and fluids well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you. You’ll finish the Bactrim at home, and we’ll send instructions for follow-up urine tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I restart my G-tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Nutrition recommends continuing your usual feeds. If you eat less than half your normal amount by mouth, give one can of 2-calorie formula through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my heart—should I get an EKG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your doctor will order a follow-up EKG to check your QT interval. Avoid any medications that can prolong it until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better. I’ll follow up with my transplant and primary care teams.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon. Take care, and call if you have any concerns.
